newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Ramos illness seen renewing focus on successor.
newsitem.headline: Ramos illness seen renewing focus on successor.

text.p: President Fidel Ramos of the Philippines is popularly known as "Steady Eddie" for his unflappable temperament and rigorous adherence to a punishing work schedule.

But his operation this week to unblock a major artery, which many called the first sign of mortality in the president, has shifted the focus to who will succeed him, political analysts said on Tuesday.
"It was a minor surgery, but for the people, the leader is completely demystified," said analyst Alex Magno, a professor at the University of the Philippines. "He's proving he's mortal after all."

"Like it or not, the political focus is no longer on Fidel Ramos, but on the person most likely to succeed him," wrote columnist Ninez Cacho-Olivares in the BusinessWorld daily. "Filipinos who believe him to be the greatest president yet will have to accept that there is life after Ramos."

Ramos was somewhat of a legend during his 40-year military career, working up to 18 hours a day, using two alarm clocks to get up before dawn, playing a mean game of golf and cutting a dash on the dance floor. If anything, he has increased the pace since taking over the presidency in 1992.

Ramos, 68, underwent surgery on Sunday to unblock his right carotid artery, one of the main passages for blood flowing to the brain. Doctors said he was in good health and was raring to get back to work, but added he would have to slow down.
That is a galling prospect in the Philippines, where displays of machismo are much admired.
"Voters very much admire Mr. Ramos," Magno said. "They will want the same work ethic from the next president, but to maintain that you need a younger person."
Ramos's illness has perhaps ended a campaign by some of his supporters to amend the constitution to enable the president to stand for a second six-year term, analysts said.

The supporters had said the economic reforms he launched, which have enabled the Philippines to join other fast-growing economies in the region, could falter when Ramos leaves office. Ramos has denied any link with the campaign and has maintained he wants to retire to a golf course.
There is no one among the list of prospective candidates for the 1998 elections who stands out, analysts say. But they add that the person to beat will be the one whom Ramos endorses.

"He needs someone who will guarantee his legacy of economic reform," said a Western diplomat in Manila. "And he doesn't want to make his choice too early, otherwise he will end up as a lame-duck president."

Vice-President Joseph Estrada, who is next in line of succession, has signalled he will be a candidate. But political analysts say the former film star is unlikely to be chosen by Ramos because of questions over his grasp of economic matters.

"Investors are concerned about the sustainability of the economic reforms that the Ramos administration has started under an Estrada rule," said Anscor Hagedorn Securities in a commentary on Tuesday. "Since the vice-president has carefully kept away from economic matters from the very beginning, people are kept wondering about his real agenda."

Analysts say Ramos' choices include House of Representatives leader Jose de Venecia and Defence Secretary Renato de Villa. Either of them would have to contest one or more opposition candidates including senators Edgardo Angara, Gloria Macapagal Arroyo and Miriam Santiago.
But none of them are sure-fire bets, and Ramos is unlikely to endorse anyone until perhaps late in 1997, they said.
